title: Service Mesh Fundamentals
summary: Why east-west traffic between your own services gets its own infrastructure layer, separate from the gateway at the edge.

slides.markdown:
A **service mesh** handles east-west traffic — service-to-service calls inside your system — with a **sidecar proxy** next to every instance.

- It buys mTLS, retries, and observability **without touching application code**.
- Split into a **data plane** (proxies moving traffic) and a **control plane** (the brain configuring them).
- It's infrastructure overhead — worth it past a certain service count, overkill below it.

slides.subTitle: The problem a gateway doesn't solve
slides.markdown:
**East-west traffic** is service-to-service calls inside your system — the orders service calling the inventory service, which calls the pricing service. A gateway only ever sees the request that entered from outside; it has no visibility into, or control over, this internal chatter.

As the number of services grows, so does the volume and complexity of this internal traffic — and each hop needs the same concerns (retries, timeouts, encryption, observability) the gateway handles at the edge, just applied internally, at a much larger number of connections.

slides.subTitle: A proxy next to every service instance
slides.markdown:
A mesh deploys a lightweight proxy (commonly **Envoy**) as a **sidecar** — a second container running alongside every service instance in the same Pod. All inbound and outbound traffic for that instance is transparently routed through its sidecar first.

Because the proxy is separate from the application container, the application code never has to know the mesh exists — retries, mTLS, and traffic shaping happen in the proxy layer, invisible to the business logic.

![Data plane vs control plane in a mesh](assets/data-plane-control-plane.svg)

The **data plane** is every sidecar proxy, actually moving and securing each request. The **control plane** (e.g. Istio's Istiod) never touches traffic directly — it computes routing rules, certificates, and policy, then pushes that configuration down to every proxy. Change a routing rule once in the control plane; every proxy picks it up.

assets.alt: Data plane vs control plane in a mesh

slides.subTitle: Without app code changes
slides.markdown:
Because the sidecar intercepts all traffic, a mesh delivers real capability with **zero application code changes**: automatic **mTLS** between every service (encrypt and authenticate every hop), **retries and timeouts** applied uniformly, and **observability** — every proxy emits consistent metrics and traces for every call, regardless of what language the service is written in.

This last point matters in a polyglot org: a Python service and a Go service get identical traffic metrics and mTLS for free, without each team separately implementing a retry library.

| | Shared library | Service mesh |
|---|---|---|
| Language coverage | One per language, must be reimplemented | Language-agnostic — proxy handles it uniformly |
| Rollout of a fix | Every service redeploys with new library version | Update the control plane / proxy version once |
| App code coupling | Tightly coupled — logic lives in the app process | Decoupled — logic lives in the sidecar |
| Overhead | None extra at runtime | An added proxy hop per call |

A shared library avoids the extra network hop but multiplies maintenance across languages and requires every service to redeploy for a fix; a mesh centralizes the fix but adds a real latency cost per call.

slides.subTitle: Adding mTLS to 20 services without touching their code
slides.markdown:
A company has 20 services across Java, Go, and Python, none with encrypted service-to-service traffic. Implementing mTLS per-service would mean 20 separate TLS integrations, certificate rotation logic, and language-specific libraries — realistically months of work with real risk of inconsistency.

Installing a mesh with sidecars instead: the control plane issues and rotates certificates automatically, and every sidecar enforces mTLS on every connection — rolled out in days, uniformly, with **zero changes** to any of the 20 services' source code.

Every sidecar is a real process consuming real CPU and memory, multiplied across every single Pod in the cluster — not a one-time cost, a per-instance one. At a few dozen services this is a rounding error; at a few thousand Pods, sidecar overhead becomes a line item worth actually budgeting for in cluster capacity planning, not an implementation detail to ignore.

This is one of the concrete costs that factors into the gateway-vs-mesh adoption threshold (see that topic's decision framework) — the mesh's benefits (uniform mTLS, retries, observability across languages) have to outweigh not just operational complexity but this compounding per-Pod resource tax.

slides.subTitle: Treating the mesh as a debugging black box
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "since the mesh handles networking transparently, app-level debugging tools are all we need — the mesh layer just works."

**Why it breaks:** a connection error, an unexpected retry, or added latency can originate in the sidecar (a misconfigured timeout, a circuit breaker tripping, an mTLS handshake failure) rather than the application — and application-only logs and traces show none of that, since the sidecar operates below the app's view entirely. Debugging purely at the app layer in a meshed system can chase a phantom app bug that's actually mesh configuration.

**The correct model:** know the sidecar's own diagnostics exist (its admin endpoint, its own metrics and logs) and check them alongside app-level signals whenever a symptom could plausibly originate in the network layer — a mesh adds a real, inspectable layer, not an invisible one.
